title: The Art of the Long-form Roguelike Run: The Nuzlocke
speaker: Stella Vermilion
summary: A lightning talk by Stella Vermilion on the Nuzlocke, a player-imposed permadeath challenge for Pokémon games, as a source of ideas for roguelikes. She covers its origin in a webcomic and its core rules, then the Pokémon systems that make it tense: per-individual stat variation, a multiplicative and heavily randomised damage formula, battles as resource attrition, encounter routing that manipulates the catch pool, and calculated sacrifices of permanently lost party members. She ends with the emotional attachment that builds through nicknamed Pokémon and their deaths.

insights.claim: The Nuzlocke began as a webcomic, 'Pokemon Hard Mode', whose two rules (release a Pokémon if it faints; catch only the first Pokémon you find in each area) turned ordinary Pokémon into a permadeath challenge.
insights.detail: Vermilion says the name comes from a panel portraying the Pokémon Nuzleaf as John Locke from Lost. The standard rules today: only catch the first Pokémon you see, fainted means dead and unusable, and the run ends when you run out. Players add nicknames for emotional attachment, plus extra rules such as no over-levelling for boss fights or no duplicate evolution lines, and there are ROM hacks built for Nuzlockers because the base games are easy.
insights.quote: You release a Pokemon if it faints and you have to catch the first Pokemon you find in an area and nothing else.

insights.claim: Nuzlockes, examined mechanically and in how they play out, contain ideas that more roguelikes could learn from or steal.
insights.detail: Vermilion runs through the high-level systems of Pokémon and Nuzlocking that explain the appeal, leaving how they apply to roguelikes partly as an exercise for the audience.
insights.quote: I think when you look at Nuzlocke both mechanically and dynamically, you see this interesting space of really cool stuff that I think more rogue likes could learn from

insights.claim: Each Pokémon is generated with hidden per-stat values (IVs of 0-31) and a nature (+10% to one stat, -10% to another), and under permadeath these small differences can decide whether a unit survives.
insights.detail: On top of a choice of four moves, these generated values make each individual different. Vermilion's example: whether an Incineroar can knock out an Aegislash before it dies can depend on whether it has maximum or minimum stats.
insights.quote: The difference between a max stat in Incinor and a minstat incinor can be the difference between life and death.

insights.claim: Pokémon combat looks like rock-paper-scissors, but its multiplicative damage formula, full of random factors and modifiers, makes it far more complex when every faint is permanent.
insights.detail: The formula includes a random roll between 85 and 100, type effectiveness, weather and battle events, items like the Life Orb, misses, critical hits, secondary effects, the enemy trainer's AI, and moves like Metronome that pick any move at random. Vermilion quotes a Northern Lion joke reducing Pokémon to rock-paper-scissors before explaining why it falls short.
insights.quote: when you factor in all of these extra factors, it becomes a lot more complex, especially because you're on such a razor's edge of life and death

insights.claim: Under Nuzlocke rules, Pokémon battles become wars of resource attrition: can you knock out the enemy team before yours is knocked out, given which of your party resists or is weak to the threat?
insights.detail: Vermilion's example from Pokémon Scarlet: against a physical flying-type attacker, her lead is nearly out, the two Pokémon that resist flying can't safely switch in, two others are weak to flying, and the last has almost no defence.
insights.quote: So battles become this war of resource attrition.

insights.claim: Nuzlocke 'encounter routing' lets players tip the odds: because already-caught species are rerolled, catching unwanted species in some areas raises the chance of finding a wanted one later.
insights.detail: In FireRed, catching the Rattata on Route 1 removes it from the pool and makes a Mankey (good against Brock) much more likely. Getting the birds on Route 1 and Route 22 nearly triples the chance of a Nidoran from 15% to 42%. Vermilion calls this one of the coolest places where players work with the RNG.
insights.quote: if you catch the Rattata on route one, it's removed from the encounter pool and suddenly the odds of finding a Mankey become much higher

insights.claim: Nuzlocke players sometimes sacrifice a Pokémon deliberately, because switching in after a knockout avoids giving the enemy a free hit, which permanently spends a resource like non-regenerating hit points in a roguelike.
insights.detail: Vermilion says sometimes there is simply no other option, but a calculated sacrifice can be the right play. Running out of Pokémon, in general or within one fight, ends the run.
insights.quote: if you switch in after a Pokemon gets knocked out that you save yourself that extra attack

insights.claim: Nuzlocke losses build emotional attachment to nicknamed party members, and victory can come after many sacrifices or even across several runs.
insights.detail: Vermilion recounts her ongoing Brilliant Diamond run: her first loss was crit at the grass gym while trying to sweep, and later two Pokémon were lost, one deliberately sacrificed so the run could continue, when she met a trainer she wasn't ready for.
insights.quote: But at the same time, we start building up these emotional attachment with these characters.
